impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder that conditions patent licenses on exclusive purchase of its unpatented products engages in unlawful tying under the Sherman Act, and whether the unpatented products must have substantial non-infringing uses to defeat an antitrust defense.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the jury's finding that Ingevity engaged in unlawful tying by conditioning licenses to its fuel vapor canister patent on customers' exclusive purchase of Ingevity's unpatented carbon honeycomb products. The court upheld the antitrust liability and corresponding damages award, finding sufficient evidence that the honeycombs had substantial non-infringing uses beyond the patent's scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors of patent holders who engage in tying arrangements can recover antitrust damages, protecting market access for rival suppliers of unpatented products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face significant antitrust exposure if they condition patent licenses on exclusive purchase of unpatented goods, even where the unpatented goods are related to the patented technology. Companies must carefully structure licensing to avoid tying liability.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a method of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's grant of JMOL invalidating Teva's headache patents, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed the patents covering use of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. The court found the specification's disclosure of one humanized antibody plus known methods of humanization was sufficient to satisfy written description and enablement for the genus claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from a more permissive standard for written description and enablement of genus claims, where the specification discloses representative species and known methods for making additional members of the genus.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar drug companies face broader patent protection for biologic drug claims, potentially delaying market entry. Companies like Lilly may face significant damages for willful infringement of antibody patents.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by emulating programs and comparing function calls to a behavioral model are directed to abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether damages may be awarded for foreign sales of infringing cybersecurity software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185M jury verdict, holding that Columbia's cybersecurity patents claiming methods for detecting malware through emulation and comparison to behavioral models are abstract at Alice step one. The court also ruled that damages for foreign software sales were improperly awarded. The case was remanded for further proceedings on step two eligibility and other issues.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing broadly-claimed software patents gain a stronger basis for challenging such patents under § 101, and the ruling limits damages exposure for foreign sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and patent holders with cybersecurity and software detection patents face heightened risk of invalidation under § 101. The decision narrows the scope of recoverable damages by excluding foreign sales.

impacts.caseName: GoTV Streaming, LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to server-side tailoring of content specifications for delivery to wireless devices based on device capabilities are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that GoTV's patents claiming methods for a server to tailor content delivery specifications to match a requesting wireless device's capabilities are ineligible for patenting under § 101. The court reversed the district court's judgment in favor of GoTV on the infringed '715 patent and entered judgment for Netflix, finding the claims directed to abstract ideas.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming and content delivery companies gain protection from infringement claims based on broadly-claimed adaptive content delivery patents, as such claims may be ineligible under § 101.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the adaptive streaming and content delivery space face increased risk that their claims will be found patent-ineligible, undermining licensing and enforcement programs.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support a jury finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether generally known information can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove its four asserted trade secrets were protectable because the information was generally known in the field. The court also reversed the patent inventorship correction, finding that the same generally known ideas could not constitute an inventive contribution. The counterfeiting claim was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against trade secret claims benefit from the ruling that generally known information in an industry cannot be protected as trade secrets, even when combined in a particular product.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for product designs must demonstrate that the specific information claimed as secret is not generally known. The ruling raises the evidentiary bar for establishing trade secret status.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on inequitable conduct in patent prosecution and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim for attempted monopolization.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact on each. The case involves allegations that Tenaris failed to disclose prior art (CYMAX documents) during prosecution of its coiled tubing patents and used those patents to attempt monopolization.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud retain the right to a full trial where facts are genuinely disputed, preventing premature disposition of complex patent-antitrust disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face ongoing exposure to both inequitable conduct defenses and Walker Process antitrust claims when prior art disclosure during prosecution is questioned, requiring careful documentation of prosecution conduct.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of a doctrine of equivalents theory for multicore processor patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement, finding error in the extraterritoriality analysis for VLSI's multicore processor patent claims against Intel. The court also reversed the striking of VLSI's damages expert theories, while affirming on certain other grounds, and remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of semiconductor and processor patents benefit from a broader view of domestic infringement, potentially capturing more of the accused infringer's activities within U.S. patent law's territorial reach.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies manufacturing processors face expanded infringement exposure when their products are designed, tested, or partially manufactured domestically, even if final assembly occurs abroad.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims relating to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the jury's infringement and damages findings were supported by sufficient evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a mixed ruling, vacating summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for the '509 and '922 patent claims. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, largely preserving a jury verdict against LG Electronics for willful infringement of digital broadcast communication patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the digital communications and broadcast standards space retain enforceability of claims tied to specific, technically-defined implementations of non-uniform constellations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers implementing broadcast standards face continued patent infringement liability, and must reassess eligibility defenses for standards-related patents after this split ruling.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watches with blood oxygen measurement features infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable pulse oximetry devices, and whether the ITC's domestic industry determination was proper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's determination that Apple violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by importing Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's wearable blood oximetry patents. The court upheld the limited exclusion order barring importation of the infringing devices, finding no error in the ITC's validity, infringement, or domestic industry analysis.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with validated wearable health technology patents can effectively use ITC proceedings to exclude infringing imports, providing powerful enforcement leverage against large consumer electronics companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics companies incorporating health-monitoring sensors into wearable devices face significant import restrictions and product redesign costs when ITC exclusion orders are affirmed.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony about historical product sales is admissible at summary judgment despite the witness's lack of personal knowledge, and whether the on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that the prior art sale expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even without personal knowledge, and rejecting the argument that the on-sale bar requires sales to expressly disclose prior art functionality. The court also held that computer source code is not hearsay.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from broader admissibility of Rule 30(b)(6) testimony to prove prior art sales, and from confirmation that the on-sale bar does not require public disclosure of the sold product's internal functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges based on historical product sales, even when direct witnesses are unavailable, lowering the evidentiary threshold for invalidation.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent that missed the deadline to seek a mandatory stay of a district court action under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a) may obtain such a stay by voluntarily dismissing and refiling the same declaratory judgment action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of a related district court action by dismissing and refiling the same declaratory judgment action. The ruling prevents manipulation of the stay mechanism in parallel ITC and district court patent proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing ITC complaints can proceed without fear that respondents will manipulate filing deadlines to obtain mandatory stays of parallel district court proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline for seeking a mandatory stay cannot reset the clock by refiling declaratory judgment actions, potentially forcing them to litigate on multiple fronts simultaneously.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB correctly construed the term 'encryption information' in claims relating to streaming partly encrypted media content, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the PTAB's claim construction of 'encryption information' in DivX's streaming media patent, vacated the Board's decision rejecting Netflix's obviousness challenge, and remanded for further proceedings under the corrected construction. The ruling impacts patent validity analysis for digital content encryption patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming technology companies challenging encryption-related patents in IPR proceedings benefit from the Federal Circuit's willingness to correct PTAB claim constructions that improperly narrow prior art applicability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with streaming and DRM-related patents face renewed invalidity challenges when the Federal Circuit reverses favorable PTAB claim constructions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the PTAB governing discretionary denial of IPR institution constitute a 'general statement of policy' exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking requirements.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's instructions guiding PTAB discretionary denials of IPR petitions are general statements of policy exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking under 5 U.S.C. § 553(b). The court emphasized that Congress provided no legal right to IPR institution and that the Director retains ultimate authority over non-institution decisions.
impacts.positiveImplications: The PTO retains broad administrative flexibility to issue and modify IPR institution guidance without formal rulemaking, enabling rapid policy adjustments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking IPR challenges to patents cannot compel formal rulemaking for PTO discretionary denial policies, limiting their ability to challenge non-institution practices through APA procedural arguments.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent plaintiff's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent infringement case against Microsoft involving Azure SmartNIC technology, and vacated the district court's summary judgment based on absence of a damages remedy. The court held the district court applied an overly rigid standard in excluding the expert's opinions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more flexible standard for admitting damages expert testimony, reducing the risk that technical errors in expert methodology will result in case-dispositive exclusions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers like Microsoft face renewed litigation exposure when appellate courts reverse Daubert exclusions of damages experts, increasing potential damages liability.

impacts.caseName: 112 Genesee Street, LLC v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Restaurant Revitalization Fund statute creates a money-mandating obligation giving the Court of Federal Claims Tucker Act jurisdiction over claims by restaurants denied RRF grants.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that over 300 restaurants stated viable Tucker Act claims against the government for failing to award RRF grants in the statutory order of application receipt. The court held that Congress's use of mandatory language ('shall award grants') created enforceable money-mandating obligations, and the SBA's failure to process applications in the required order was actionable.
impacts.positiveImplications: Small businesses denied pandemic relief grants under mandatory federal programs have a viable damages claim against the government where the statute uses mandatory language directing grant awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: The government faces potential liability for hundreds of millions in unpaid RRF grants, establishing precedent that mandatory statutory grant language creates enforceable claims even after program funds are exhausted.
